title: Homeostasis
summary: How negative feedback keeps the internal environment within narrow limits, using blood glucose and body temperature as examples, plus the kidney's role in osmoregulation.

keyterms.definition: Maintenance of the internal environment of an organism within narrow limits, e.g. body temperature, blood pH, glucose and solute concentration.
Control mechanism in which a change from the set point triggers responses that return the variable towards the set point.
Hormone secreted by beta cells of the pancreatic islets when blood glucose is high; stimulates glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis.
Hormone secreted by alpha cells of the pancreatic islets when blood glucose is low; stimulates glycogen breakdown in the liver.
Diabetes caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells, so little or no insulin is produced.
Diabetes in which target cells become insensitive to insulin; linked to obesity, diet, inactivity and genetic factors.
Sensory receptor that detects temperature; peripheral ones in the skin and central ones in the hypothalamus.
Narrowing of arterioles supplying skin capillaries, reducing blood flow near the surface and so reducing heat loss.
Fat tissue whose mitochondria carry out uncoupled respiration, releasing energy as heat instead of producing ATP.
Thyroid hormone that increases metabolic rate and so heat production; its secretion is regulated via the hypothalamus and pituitary.
Control of the water balance and solute concentration of the blood and body fluids.
Filtration of blood under high pressure in the glomerulus, separating small molecules into the filtrate while retaining cells and proteins.
Return of useful substances (all glucose and amino acids, most water and ions) from filtrate to blood, mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule.
Nephron loop whose ascending limb actively pumps sodium ions into the medulla, creating a hypertonic medulla.
Antidiuretic hormone, released from the posterior pituitary when blood solute concentration is high; increases water permeability of collecting ducts.
Channel protein allowing rapid water movement through membranes; inserted into collecting duct membranes in response to ADH.

questions.prompt: Which variable is NOT normally kept within narrow limits by homeostasis in humans?
options: Body core temperature
Blood pH
Heart rate
Blood glucose concentration
questions.explanation: Homeostasis maintains the internal environment (temperature, pH, glucose, osmotic concentration). Heart rate is deliberately varied, e.g. rising in exercise, to help keep those variables stable.

questions.statement: In negative feedback, a deviation from the set point causes a response that amplifies the deviation.
questions.explanation: That describes positive feedback. Negative feedback reverses the change, returning the variable towards the set point.

questions.prompt: Order the events after a carbohydrate-rich meal.
items: Beta cells in the pancreatic islets detect the rise
Insulin is secreted into the blood
Liver, muscle and adipose cells take up glucose
Blood glucose returns towards the set point
questions.explanation: This negative feedback loop uses insulin as the signal; target cells increase glucose uptake and convert it to glycogen or fat.

questions.text: When blood glucose is low, alpha cells secrete ___, which stimulates the liver to break down glycogen.
questions.explanation: Glucagon triggers glycogenolysis in liver cells, releasing glucose into the blood. Note glycogen is the stored polysaccharide, not the hormone.

questions.prompt: Match each item to its role in blood glucose regulation.

pairs.right: Stores glucose as glycogen and releases it
Stimulates cells to take up glucose

questions.explanation: The islets of Langerhans contain both cell types. The liver is the main target that can both store and release glucose.

questions.prompt: What is the cause of type 1 diabetes?
options: Target cells become insensitive to insulin
The immune system destroys insulin-secreting beta cells
Too much glucagon is secreted
The liver cannot store glycogen
questions.explanation: Type 1 is an autoimmune condition, usually starting in childhood. Without insulin, glucose cannot be taken up by cells, so it is treated with insulin injections.

questions.prompt: Which statement about type 2 diabetes is correct?
options: It is always treated with insulin injections from diagnosis
It is caused by an infection of the pancreas
Target cells respond less to insulin; risk factors include obesity, inactivity and genetic factors
It only occurs in children
questions.explanation: In type 2 diabetes insulin is often produced but target cells show insulin resistance. It is first managed with diet, exercise and drugs.

questions.statement: In both types of diabetes, blood glucose concentration remains abnormally high after meals.
questions.explanation: Whether insulin is missing (type 1) or ineffective (type 2), cells take up less glucose, so hyperglycaemia results.

questions.text: Insulin and glucagon reach their target cells by being transported in the ___.
questions.explanation: Hormones are secreted by endocrine glands directly into the blood and act on cells with the specific receptors.

questions.prompt: Why is negative feedback suitable for homeostasis?
options: It keeps the variable fluctuating around a set point
It drives the variable continuously upward
It requires no receptors
It only works through the nervous system
questions.explanation: Receptors detect changes, and effectors counteract them. The variable oscillates within narrow limits around the set point; both hormones and nerves can be involved.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain acts as the control centre for thermoregulation?
options: Cerebellum
Medulla oblongata
Pituitary gland
Hypothalamus
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus receives impulses from peripheral thermoreceptors, has its own central thermoreceptors, and coordinates responses via nerves and the pituitary.

questions.prompt: Match each thermoregulation response to the condition that triggers it.

pairs.right: Body too cold: muscle contractions generate heat
Body too hot: evaporation removes heat
Body too cold: brown fat releases heat

questions.explanation: Responses to heat increase heat loss; responses to cold reduce heat loss or increase heat production.

questions.statement: During vasoconstriction, skin capillaries themselves contract to reduce blood flow.
questions.explanation: Capillaries have no muscle. Smooth muscle in the walls of arterioles supplying the skin contracts, narrowing them and diverting blood away from the surface.

questions.text: In brown adipose tissue, respiration is ___, so energy is released as heat rather than used to make ATP.
questions.explanation: A protein in the inner mitochondrial membrane lets protons flow back without passing through ATP synthase, so the energy is lost as heat. Brown fat is important in newborns.

questions.prompt: How does thyroxine help raise body temperature?
options: It causes vasodilation
It increases metabolic rate, so more heat is produced by respiration
It stimulates sweat glands
It directly causes shivering
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus stimulates the pituitary to secrete TSH, which stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine. Thyroxine raises the metabolic rate of many tissues.

questions.prompt: Order the events when a person enters a cold environment.
items: Peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin detect cold
Nerve impulses travel to the hypothalamus
Skin arterioles constrict and skeletal muscles shiver
Heat loss decreases and heat production increases
questions.explanation: Receptor → control centre → effectors → response is the general pattern of a negative feedback loop.

questions.statement: Hair erection traps an insulating layer of air, though the effect is small in humans.
questions.explanation: Contraction of erector muscles raises hairs. In furry mammals this traps a thick layer of air; in humans it only produces 'goosebumps'.

questions.prompt: Why does sweating cool the body?
options: Sweat is colder than the body
Sweat reflects sunlight
Evaporation of water from sweat absorbs heat from the skin
Sweat glands use up heat when they secrete
questions.explanation: Water has a high latent heat of vaporization, so evaporating sweat removes a large amount of heat from the skin surface.

questions.text: The hypothalamus controls thyroxine secretion indirectly via the ___ gland.
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus signals the anterior pituitary to release TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland.

questions.prompt: Why is thermoregulation an example of negative feedback?
options: Responses to a fall in temperature raise it, and responses to a rise lower it
Responses always increase body temperature
Temperature changes are amplified until a peak is reached
It involves hormones only
questions.explanation: Each response opposes the detected change, bringing core temperature back towards about 37 °C. Both nerves and hormones are involved.

questions.prompt: What creates the high blood pressure in the glomerulus that drives ultrafiltration?
options: The efferent arteriole is wider than the afferent arteriole
Podocytes pump blood into Bowman's capsule
The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole
Active transport of water into the capsule
questions.explanation: Blood enters through a wider vessel than it leaves by, so pressure builds in the glomerulus and forces fluid out into Bowman's capsule.

questions.prompt: Match each structure to its role in ultrafiltration.

pairs.right: Pores let fluid leave the blood
Cells with filtration slits around capillaries

questions.explanation: Together these layers let water, glucose, amino acids, ions and urea pass but hold back blood cells and most proteins.

questions.statement: Glucose is normally absent from urine because all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
questions.explanation: Glucose is filtered but completely reabsorbed by co-transport with sodium ions in the PCT. Glucose in urine indicates blood glucose exceeds the reabsorption capacity, as in untreated diabetes.

questions.prompt: Which adaptation of proximal convoluted tubule cells increases the rate of selective reabsorption?
options: Few mitochondria
Thick walls with several cell layers
Impermeability to water
Microvilli and many mitochondria
questions.explanation: Microvilli increase the surface area for absorption, and mitochondria supply ATP for active transport of sodium ions and co-transport of glucose and amino acids.

questions.text: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle actively pumps sodium ions out but is impermeable to ___.
questions.explanation: Because water cannot follow, the medulla's interstitial fluid becomes hypertonic. This lets water be drawn out of the descending limb and collecting ducts by osmosis.

items: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise
Aquaporins are inserted into collecting duct membranes
More water is reabsorbed into the hypertonic medulla
A small volume of concentrated urine is produced
questions.explanation: ADH makes collecting ducts permeable to water, so water moves by osmosis into the hypertonic medulla and is returned to the blood.

questions.statement: When a person drinks a large volume of water, ADH secretion increases.
questions.explanation: Excess water dilutes the blood, so ADH secretion falls. Collecting ducts become less permeable, and a large volume of dilute urine is produced.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes excretion from osmoregulation?
options: Excretion removes metabolic waste such as urea; osmoregulation controls water and solute balance
Excretion controls blood water content; osmoregulation removes urea
Both terms mean the removal of faeces
Osmoregulation occurs only in the bladder
questions.explanation: The kidney does both: it excretes nitrogenous waste (urea) made by metabolism and adjusts the amount of water and ions lost to keep body fluid concentration constant.

questions.text: ADH acts on collecting duct cells, causing vesicles containing ___ to fuse with the membrane.
questions.explanation: More water channels in the membrane increase permeability, allowing more water reabsorption by osmosis.

questions.prompt: How does blood flow change from rest to vigorous exercise?
options: Flow to the brain increases greatly and flow to muscles stays constant
Flow to skeletal muscles increases greatly, flow to the gut and kidneys decreases, and flow to the brain stays roughly constant
Flow to all organs increases equally
Flow to the gut increases to supply more glucose
questions.explanation: Arterioles to active muscles dilate while those to the gut and kidneys constrict, redirecting blood. The brain's supply is kept almost constant in all states, including sleep.
